```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(BUCSS)
```

Once a planner has returned, how do you read the plan, pull the one number you
need out of it, or collect it into a table or a manuscript? Every `ss_buc_*`
function returns the same kind of object: a tidy result of class `bucss_plan`,
holding a bias and uncertainty corrected plan (Anderson, Kelley, & Maxwell,
2017). This vignette shows the three ways to read it, which follow the same
conventions as the **DMAR** package, so the habits carry over.

We will use a two-way between-subjects ANOVA throughout.

```{r}
result <- ss_buc_factorial_anova(F_observed = 5, N = 120, levels_A = 2,
                                 levels_B = 3, effect = "factor_B")
```

## 1. Read It as a Printed Summary

Printing the object shows the aligned `term`/`value` table, in the **DMAR**
style: the design results first (the necessary sample size, named for its
unit; the implied total sample size for per-group and per-cell designs; the
achieved power at the returned size; the bias and uncertainty adjusted
noncentrality parameter; and the planning effect size, the effect size the
plan is built on, in the design's usual metric), then the rows echoing the
planning inputs you supplied. Footer lines close with the design, for the regression planners the
predictor frame (`random_predictors`), the unit the sample size is counted in,
and the largest assurance this prior result can support.

```{r}
result
```

Displayed values are rounded for reading (whole numbers print clean; other
values print at three significant figures); the stored values keep full
precision. Change the display with `options(bucss.digits = )`, and put back
whatever was set before when you are done:

```{r}
old <- options(bucss.digits = 5)
result
options(old)  # restore the previous setting
```

## 2. Pull a Single Number Out

The object is an ordinary `data.frame` with a character `term` column and a
numeric `value` column, so you can index it like any data frame. The design
results come first (here `necessary_n_per_cell`, `total_N`, `actual_power`,
`ncp_adjusted`, and `f_planning`; the size row is `necessary_n_per_group` or
`necessary_N` in other designs, and the planning effect size row is named for
its metric), followed by one row per planning input, so the assumptions
travel with the result through subsetting and `write.csv()`.

```{r}
result$value[result$term == "necessary_n_per_cell"]
result$value[result$term == "total_N"]
```

That works for any row. For the sample size and its power, `tidy()` below
gives them directly, and `glance()` puts every row in a column of its own, so
any single value can be pulled out by name.

## 3. The Broom Verbs: `tidy()` and `glance()`

`tidy()` returns the compact estimate view, the same shape as **DMAR**'s
sample size planners: one row with `term` (`"sample_size"`), `estimate` (the
necessary sample size in the design's unit), and `power` (the achieved power
at that size).

```{r}
tidy(result)
tidy(result)$estimate
```

`glance()` returns the one-row wide view. It begins with the same `term`,
`estimate`, and `power` columns as `tidy()` (as **DMAR**'s planners do), then
gives every quantity and echoed planning input a column of its own, and ends
with the design, the effect tested, the unit, the planned test's degrees of
freedom, and the assurance ceiling. It is the convenient shape for pulling one
value out by name or collecting many results into one table for reporting.

```{r}
glance(result)
glance(result)$ncp_adjusted
```

Both verbs come from the **generics** package and are re-exported by BUCSS, so
they work as soon as the package is loaded, with no extra setup. The full
precision values are always available in the object itself, since only the
printed display rounds. And for a manuscript's method section,
`planning_sentence()` writes the sentence:

```{r}
planning_sentence(result)
```

## The Planning Effect Size

The noncentrality parameter is the natural scale for the correction, but it is
not the scale a paper reports an effect on, and it grows with the sample size.
So every plan also carries its **planning effect size**: the effect size the
plan is built on, which is `ncp_adjusted` restated in the design's usual
metric. It sits directly after `ncp_adjusted`, and its name says which metric
it is:

| Planner | Row | Metric |
|---------|-----|--------|
| `ss_buc_independent_t` (`ss_buc_smd`) | `smd_planning` | standardized mean difference |
| `ss_buc_welch_t` | `smd_planning` | standardized mean difference, standardized by the root mean square of the two standard deviations |
| `ss_buc_paired_t` (`ss_buc_smd_paired`) | `dz_planning` | standardized mean of the paired differences |
| `ss_buc_one_sample_t` | `std_mean_planning` | standardized mean |
| the eight ANOVA and ANCOVA planners | `f_planning` | Cohen's *f* for the effect, relative to its own error term |
| `ss_buc_reg_coef`, `ss_buc_reg_joint` | `f2_planning` | Cohen's *f* squared |
| `ss_buc_R2` | `R2_planning` | squared multiple correlation |
| `ss_buc_correlation` | `rho_planning` | correlation |
| `ss_buc_manova` | `D2_planning` | squared Mahalanobis distance |
| `ss_buc_chisq_diff` | `rmsea_d_planning` | root mean square error of approximation of the difference test |

For the example above, the published result was *F*(2, 114) = 5, whose sample
Cohen's *f* is `sqrt(5 * 2/114)`, about `r format(signif(sqrt(10 / 114), 3))`.
The plan is built on a much smaller effect:

```{r}
f_planning <- result$value[result$term == "f_planning"]
f_planning
f_planning^2 / (1 + f_planning^2)  # the same effect as a partial eta squared
```

"Built on" is meant literally. `actual_power` is the ordinary power of a study
of the returned size when the population effect is the planning effect size,
so any power calculator reproduces it from the effect alone. Here the planned
study has `r result$value[result$term == "total_N"]` participants in 6 cells,
and its test of the effect has 2 and
`r result$value[result$term == "total_N"] - 6` degrees of freedom:

```{r}
total_N <- result$value[result$term == "total_N"]
1 - pf(qf(.95, 2, total_N - 6), 2, total_N - 6, ncp = total_N * f_planning^2)
result$value[result$term == "actual_power"]
```

A few things to know when you carry the planning effect size elsewhere:

* **It is the value the plan is built on, not a better estimate of the
  effect.** With `alpha_prior = 1` and `assurance = .5` it is a median
  unbiased estimate; at a higher assurance it is deliberately smaller, an
  effect the plan must still be powered for, so report it as the planning
  effect size rather than as the size of the effect.
* **Within-subjects and split-plot designs.** There `f_planning` is relative
  to the effect's own error term, which already reflects the correlation among
  the repeated measures. Power functions that take an *f* standardized by the
  raw scores together with a correlation (such as **DMAR**'s
  `ss_power_rm_anova()` and `ss_power_split_plot_anova()`) expect a different
  number; each planner's help page gives the conversion. With `epsilon` below
  1 the planning effect size stays on the sphericity scale, like
  `ncp_adjusted`, and `actual_power` is the power under the same sphericity
  correction.
* **Regression with sampled predictors.** With `random_predictors = TRUE`,
  `f2_planning` and `R2_planning` are the population values when the
  predictors are sampled along with the outcome, and `actual_power` is the
  power in that frame.
* **An unbalanced prior study.** When the planner reduces the prior study to
  a balanced design in two ways and reports the smaller noncentrality
  parameter, the planning effect size belongs to that same balanced design. An
  ordinary power analysis at it can then return a slightly smaller sample size
  than the plan, never a larger one, because the plan is the larger of the two
  designs' requirements.

`planning_sentence()` names the planning effect size in its second sentence,
as shown in the previous section.

## What Lives Where

* Every planning result and every echoed input is a row of the `value`
  column: the design results (the size row named for its unit, `total_N`,
  `actual_power`, `ncp_adjusted`, and the planning effect size) and the
  planning inputs. Rows survive any
  further arithmetic, subsetting, or export you do on the object. A switch
  such as the regression planners' `random_predictors` is echoed as 1 (`TRUE`)
  or 0 (`FALSE`), since the value column is numeric, and the print method's
  footer names it in words. The within-subjects and split-plot planners echo
  `epsilon`, the sphericity parameter the plan assumed (1 under sphericity),
  for every effect it applies to.
* Everything else travels on attributes: the design label, the effect tested,
  and the unit, which are text, and the assurance ceiling and the planned
  test's degrees of freedom, which are numbers describing the prior result and
  the planned test rather than rows of the plan. All of it is surfaced by
  `glance()`, and the design (with the effect tested), the unit, and the
  ceiling by the print method's footer.

## References

Anderson, S. F., Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2017). Sample-size planning for
more accurate statistical power: A method adjusting sample effect sizes for
publication bias and uncertainty. *Psychological Science, 28*, 1547--1562.
https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617723724
